subject: Copywriting
title: I Have a Dream
description: A quick win: understand I Have a Dream.

hook.text: Martin Luther King Jr.'s most famous line was improvised. 'I Have a Dream' wasn't in his prepared text.

buildup.text: Mahalia Jackson shouted 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' from behind the podium. He abandoned his notes.

discovery.text: The phrase used repetition—anaphora. 'I have a dream...' repeated eight times, each vision bigger than the last.

twist.text: King's speechwriter told him not to use the dream bit. He'd used it before and it was 'trite.' Kings instinct won.

climax.text: 250,000 people heard it live. Billions have heard it since. Four words became the headline of the civil rights era.

punchline.text: Four improvised words. The defining headline of a movement.

quiz.question: Who encouraged King to talk about the dream during his speech?

details.summary: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963 used its title phrase as a rhetorical headline that defined the civil rights movement. The repetition of 'I have a dream' created a rhythmic, escalating structure that made the vision concrete, personal, and unforgettable.
details.whyItMatters: The phrase demonstrates how a headline can encapsulate an entire movement's aspiration. Its structure — personal declaration plus specific vision — offers a template for any message of hope and change.
takeaways: The repeated phrase created rhythmic escalation and emotional momentum
Personal declaration ('I') made an abstract cause feel intimate
Each repetition painted a more specific and vivid picture of the future

faq.question: Why is 'I Have a Dream' so effective as a headline?
faq.answer: It is personal (I), aspirational (dream), and present tense (have). The phrase invites listeners into a shared vision. Each repetition adds a specific detail, making the abstract dream increasingly concrete and emotionally overwhelming.

faq.question: Was 'I Have a Dream' planned or improvised?
faq.answer: The 'dream' section was partially improvised. King's prepared text was different, but Mahalia Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream!'
